overview:
Joshua gathers all the tribes at Shechem and speaks for the LORD, retelling Israel's story in God's own voice: Terah's family serving other gods beyond the River, the call of Abraham, Egypt and the sea, the Amorites, Balaam, Jericho, and a land they did not labor for. Then he puts the choice: serve the LORD, or choose this day the gods of the fathers or of the Amorites; he and his house will serve the LORD. The people insist they will serve him. Joshua warns they cannot, for he is holy and jealous, and they insist again. Joshua makes a covenant, writes the words in the book of the law, and sets up a great stone as witness. Then come three burials: Joshua, Joseph's bones, and Eleazar.

The choice reaches back to Israel's own beginnings. The gods to be put away are first of all the ones “your fathers served” (vv. 2, 14–15).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named, though v. 26 says Joshua “wrote these words in the book of the law of God.” The Talmud credits Joshua, with his death added by Eleazar and Phinehas; many scholars see a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Joshua's lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The end of Joshua's life, at 110 (v. 29): about 1380 BC by the reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1; many scholars prefer the 12th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Shechem, between Mounts Ebal and Gerizim, at “the sanctuary of the LORD” under an oak (v. 26). The Septuagint reads Shiloh. Burials at Timnath-serah, Shechem, and the hill of Phinehas in Ephraim.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Judges 2:6–9 (Joshua's death and burial retold); Genesis 35:2–4 (Jacob puts away foreign gods at Shechem); Genesis 50:25 and Exodus 13:19 (Joseph's bones).

hermeneutics:
The two cities of Terah's story were the great centers of the moon god. Ur, where the family began (Genesis 11:31), had the temple of Nanna, the Sumerian moon god, beside its ziggurat. Harran, where Terah stopped and died, had the temple of Sin, the same god under his Akkadian name, rebuilt as late as the 6th century BC by the Babylonian king Nabonidus, whose mother served there. When v. 2 says Israel's fathers “served other gods” beyond the River, a hearer would think of real cults in real places. Israel's covenant does not begin with a people raised on the true God. It begins with a family that had to leave its gods behind, and v. 14 asks each generation to do the same.

Shechem already had a temple. In 1926 Ernst Sellin uncovered a massive fortress temple at Tell Balata, and in front of it stood a great limestone standing stone, the largest found in the land. Lawrence Stager has argued that the building remained in use into Iron Age I and is the “house of the god Berith” (“lord of the covenant”) of Judges 9:46, where Abimelech's story is set. Some scholars have suggested that the standing stone could be Joshua's “great stone” (v. 26) and the “pillar” of Judges 9:6. The identification remains a possibility, not a consensus. Either way, Joshua renews the covenant at a city where covenant gods were worshiped, and within a generation Shechem's own covenant shrine belongs to Baal (Judges 9:4).

structure.summary: Alternating speeches (A B A B): after God's history of Israel, Joshua and the people answer each other four times, framed by the history and the covenant ceremony.

notes: **Serve:** the Hebrew verb *avad* occurs 16 times in the chapter, 14 of them in the dialogue of vv. 14–24. Each round of the exchange ends with the people saying it again.
**Beyond the River:** the phrase comes four times (vv. 2, 3, 14, 15), tying the call to choose back to the fathers' gods. KJV renders the River (the Euphrates) as “the flood.”
**Witness:** the people are witnesses against themselves (v. 22, twice), and the stone is a witness because “it hath heard” (v. 27, twice).

The book's last scene. Chapter 23 warned the leaders; chapter 24 binds the whole people by covenant and then closes three lives, the leader, the patriarch whose bones came out of Egypt, and the priest. Verse 31 hands the story to the elders who outlived Joshua, the point where Judges takes it up.

**Backward and forward:** at the same Shechem oak Jacob buried his household's foreign gods (Genesis 35:4), and Joseph's bones rest in the field Jacob bought there (Genesis 33:19). Judges 2:6–9 repeats Joshua's death and burial, and Judges 9 returns to Shechem's pillar and temple.

traditions.text: Mormon explains why the Nephite judges could not punish Korihor for his teaching: there was no law against a man's belief, for, he writes, the scripture says, “Choose ye this day, whom ye will serve.” He reads v. 15 as a principle of law. Serving God was a person's privilege, and unbelief was not a crime, while murder, theft, and adultery were.

The same call appears long before Joshua in the Restoration account of Enoch. The Lord sends Enoch to preach with the words, “Choose ye this day, to serve the Lord God who made you.” Joshua's challenge at Shechem becomes one instance of a call God has issued since the earliest generations.

Verse 2 says only that Terah and his fathers “served other gods.” The Book of Abraham fills in the picture: Abraham's fathers had turned to the gods of Elkenah, Libnah, Mahmackrah, Korash, and Pharaoh, and tried to sacrifice Abraham himself. Terah repented for a time during a famine, but once settled in Haran he “turned again unto his idolatry.” The Church's footnotes link v. 2 to Abraham 2:5 and v. 14 to Abraham 1:5–7.

A thematic link. At the waters of Mormon, Alma invites believers to be baptized “as a witness before him” that they have covenanted to serve God and keep his commandments. At Shechem the people are their own witnesses that they have chosen to serve the LORD (v. 22). In both, serving God is the content of the covenant and the people's own act is its witness.

The Greek text sets the assembly and covenant at Shiloh, before the tabernacle, not Shechem (vv. 1, 25), while still burying Joseph at Shechem. After Joshua's burial it adds that the stone knives he used to circumcise Israel at Gilgal were put in the tomb with him and remain there “unto this day.” It closes with lines the Hebrew lacks: Israel carries the ark about among them, Phinehas succeeds Eleazar, and the people turn to Astarte and are given into the hand of Eglon of Moab, the opening of Judges 3.

Like the Septuagint, this retelling places the covenant at Shiloh, on the 16th day of the third month, near the feast of Weeks. God's history begins with one rock out of which Abraham and Nahor were hewn (Isaiah 51:1–2), and Abraham's vision of Genesis 15 becomes a revelation of the place of fire for the wicked and torches of light for the righteous. The people answer, “The Lord is our God, and him only will we serve,” and celebrate for twenty-eight days.

Pseudo-Philo has Israel lament Joshua as “the wing of this swift eagle” and bury him with their own hands. The Talmud tells the opposite story. The hill Gaash (v. 30) means “quaking,” Rav says, because the mountain raged to kill the people for failing to eulogize Joshua properly, and anyone slow to mourn a sage deserves the same.

Josephus gives Joshua's 110 years as forty with Moses, learning, and twenty-five as commander after him, and praises his wisdom, eloquence, and courage. He was buried at Timnath in Ephraim. Eleazar died about the same time, leaving the high priesthood to Phinehas, and his tomb was at Gabatha.

Why bury Joseph at Shechem? Rabbi Hama son of Rabbi Hanina answers that Joseph's brothers took him from Shechem (Genesis 37:12–28), so to Shechem Israel returned what had been lost. The Talmud also notes that Exodus 13:19 credits Moses with carrying the bones while v. 32 credits the children of Israel, and concludes that whoever finishes a deed gets the credit for it.

What did Joshua write “in the book of the law” (v. 26)? Two rabbis disagree: one says the last eight verses of Deuteronomy, on Moses' death; the other says the chapter on the cities of refuge, which Joshua copied into his own book. Rashi adds the Targum's reading that Joshua laid his words up beside the Torah scroll, and identifies the oak as the one under which Jacob buried the strange gods at Shechem.

Augustine reads the people's confidence in v. 21 as boasting: Joshua had warned that they could not serve a holy God, and they relied on themselves instead of seeking grace, as Romans later teaches. The stone that “hath heard” (v. 27) is set up visibly, he says, but must be understood spiritually, and the covenant points ahead to the new covenant.

Eusebius says Joshua's tomb was still pointed out in his day near the village of Thamna, north of Mount Gaas. He also places the oak of Shechem, where Abimelech was made king, in the outskirts of Neapolis toward the tomb of Joseph, so that the oak, the stone, and the grave of v. 32 were all remembered as one neighborhood.

In his memorial of Paula's pilgrimage, Jerome says she visited the tombs of Joshua and Eleazar in the hill country of Ephraim, facing each other, Joshua's at Timnath-serah north of Gaash and Eleazar's on the hill of Phinehas. She was surprised that the man who divided the whole land had chosen such rough and rocky ground for himself.
